title: East Asia’s manufacturing escalator has slowed – AI alone will not restart it
gist: Citing the World Bank's 'Riding the AI Wave' update, Mia Mikic notes East Asia exported US$1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in 12 months, lifting 2026 growth forecasts, but most value (design, IP, software) is captured elsewhere and AI hardware creates few jobs. The boom rests on revocable US tariff exemptions and a >US$1 trillion hyperscaler capex cycle that could reverse, while AI trade rules are set without developing countries.

themes.theme: East Asia's AI hardware export boom

insights.claim: According to the World Bank, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam exported US$1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months to April 2026.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: Quantifies how heavily East Asian trade now depends on the AI capex cycle.

insights.claim: The design, software, intellectual property and data that make AI hardware valuable are largely created and captured outside the East Asian exporting countries, so what matters is which tasks a country performs rather than which products it ships.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: Value capture in the AI supply chain accrues to IP holders, not regional assemblers.

themes.theme: Jobs and the stalled manufacturing escalator

insights.claim: The World Bank acknowledges manufacturing's role as an escalator moving workers into better-paid work has slowed, with countries hitting peak industrial employment shares in 2015 and 2019 at incomes of roughly US$900 to US$5,900 per head.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: Premature deindustrialisation caps the growth upside for emerging Asian economies.
insights.locator: Manufacturing was not only good for exports

insights.claim: In Malaysia, data centres require RM4.6 million of investment per job created, versus less than RM1 million for electronics and automotive jobs.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: Data-centre investment booms deliver capex and power demand but little employment, limiting political and consumption spillovers.

insights.claim: Services already account for roughly 26-33% of the value of global manufactured exports, yet the World Bank's AI trade figures omit AI-related services such as software development, business process outsourcing and data work.

insights.so_what: Official AI trade data understate services exposure, where the Philippines and Vietnam are building capabilities.

insights.claim: Mikic argues emerging economies should compete on tasks rather than sectors, prioritise openness to services, technology and ideas over cheap labour and scale, and reform services regulation.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: Countries reforming services regulation may be better long-term growth bets than pure assembly hubs.
insights.quote: Openness still works, but openness to services, technology and ideas now matters more than cheap labour and economies of scale.

insights.claim: Most AI-related goods remain exempt from US tariffs, but the author warns that what is granted unilaterally can be withdrawn unilaterally.

insights.so_what: Withdrawal of US tariff exemptions is a key downside risk for Asian AI hardware exporters.

insights.claim: Rules deciding who captures value from AI — on cross-border data flows, digital services, standards and export controls — are being written unilaterally or in bilateral and mini-plurilateral deals, with most developing countries having little say.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: AI value capture is being locked in by dominant powers outside multilateral forums.

insights.claim: Developing countries asking the UN for a voice in AI standards are effectively making a trade-policy demand, and treating AI governance and trade governance separately suits those who already dominate both.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: AI standards debates at the UN are proxy fights over trade rules and market access.

insights.claim: At the UN General Assembly, Brazil and France worried about AI power concentrated in a few firms and states, developing countries sought access to compute and standard-setting, and the United States treated AI dominance as a strategic and economic imperative.
insights.speaker: Mia Mikic
insights.so_what: Divergent national AI stances signal a fragmented global regulatory landscape.
